hints: Remember when a real gas acts most like an ideal gas, think about high temperature and low pressure to minimise attractions and particle volume.
Compare the conditions first, two gases are at 1000 K and low or high pressure, while the other two are at cold 250 K.
Now compare the particles left at hot, low pressure conditions, a non-polar molecule with only weak London forces will be more ideal than a polar one.
walkthrough:
**Recall the ideal conditions**

Think like a particle. An ideal gas assumes no attractions between particles and negligible particle volume.

Real gases get closest to this at high temperature (particles move fast, attractions matter less) and low pressure (particles far apart):
$$\text{ideal behaviour} \approx \text{high } T + \text{low } p + \text{weak intermolecular forces}$$

**Sort by temperature and pressure**

Look at the table. High T is 1000 K, low p is $1.00 \times 10^5$ Pa.

Only one substance has both: $\text{N}_2$ at 1000 K and $1.00 \times 10^5$ Pa. The others are either cold (250 K) or squeezed to $1.00 \times 10^6$ Pa, or both.

**Check the type of particle**

Even at the same conditions, polarity matters. $\text{HCl}$ is polar with permanent dipole-dipole forces, while $\text{N}_2$ is non-polar with only weak London dispersion forces.

So hot, low pressure plus non-polar $\text{N}_2$ gives the closest match to ideal behaviour.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CO}_2$ is at low 250 K. Cold particles move slowly so intermolecular attractions become significant, causing deviation from ideal behaviour.
options.B: Incorrect. Although temperature is high at 1000 K, pressure is high at $1.00 \times 10^6$ Pa and $\text{HCl}$ is polar. High pressure forces particles close together and dipole-dipole forces cause strong deviation.
options.C: Correct. $\text{N}_2$ is at high temperature (1000 K) and low pressure ($1.00 \times 10^5$ Pa) and is non-polar with only weak London forces. Fast-moving, widely spaced particles with minimal attraction behave most ideally.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{O}_2$ is at the worst combination: low 250 K and high $1.00 \times 10^6$ Pa. Cold, closely packed particles show maximum deviation from ideal assumptions.
